Melk
MELK
n. (the Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1089 on the Danube, source of the fifteenth-century Melk reform)
Slavic Medilica, a boundary place, through Old High German Medelike.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Melk stands on a rock over the Danube, where Leopold II of Babenberg gave his castle to Benedictine monks in 1089. In the fifteenth century it became the centre of the Melk reform, a movement that spread through the Austrian and south German houses, restoring the rule where it had lapsed, rebuilding libraries and reforming discipline from the inside without waiting for a pope or a council. Between 1702 and 1746 Jakob Prandtauer rebuilt the whole abbey as the best-known baroque monastery in Europe. The dictionary records Melk for that reform, because self-correction inside an institution is the rarest thing in church history and Scripture requires it by name. The charge laid on a church that has slipped begins with a diagnosis of affection rather than of practice, “because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4), and the remedy prescribed is a return to what was done at the start, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5). The prophetic summons is likewise backward before it is forward, “Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts” (Mal 3:7), and the end in view is a church presented clean, “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle” (Eph 5:27).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reform as a change from worse to better; discipline as instruction and government; a rule as a prescribed form of conduct; to repent as to feel sorrow for sin with amendment; and a visitation as the act of a superior who inspects.

expand to see more

REFORM, v.t. To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.

DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement.

RULE, n. A prescribed form or standard of conduct or practice; government; sway.

REPENT, v.i. To sorrow or be pained for sin, as a violation of God's holy law, with amendment of life.

VISITATION, n. The act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation or religious house to inspect.

Key Scripture

Rev 2:4 — "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love."

Rev 2:5 — "Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent."

Mal 3:7 — "Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return?"

Eph 5:27 — "That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish."

Modern Corruption

Lower Austrian Benedictine abbey of 1089 whose fifteenth-century reform restored the rule across the Austrian and south German houses.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an institution can reform itself from the inside, and that Scripture asks exactly that of a slipping church. Melk did it in the fifteenth century without waiting for Rome, and the diagnosis Christ gives such a house concerns its affections, “Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee” (Rev 2:4).

The live temptation is a reform of discipline that never reaches the heart, which leaves a tidier house and the same disease. The prescribed remedy is deliberately retrospective, “and do the first works” (Rev 2:5); the prophetic call is a turning back before it is a going forward, “Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances” (Mal 3:7); and the end Christ has in view is a bride without blemish rather than an abbey without scandal, “but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph 5:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek metanoeo (G3340), to repent; Greek mnemoneuo (G3421), to remember; Hebrew shub (H7725), to return; Greek spilos (G4696), a spot, a blemish.

expand to see more

Greek agape (G0026) — love; “because thou hast left thy first love”, Revelation 2:4.

Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to repent, to change the mind; “and repent, and do the first works”, Revelation 2:5.

Greek mnemoneuo (G3421) — to remember, to call to mind; “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen”, Revelation 2:5.

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, to return; “Return unto me, and I will return unto you”, Malachi 3:7.

Greek spilos (G4696) — a spot, a stain, a blemish; “not having spot, or wrinkle”, Ephesians 5:27.

Usage

"“because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4) — the diagnosis a slipping house gets."

"“and do the first works” (Rev 2:5) — a remedy that looks backward."

"“a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle” (Eph 5:27) — the end actually in view."
